{{short description|Term in mathematics}}
{{Lie groups|expanded={{Lie groups |expanded=all}}}}

In the [[mathematics|mathematical]] study of [[Lie algebra]]s and [[Lie group]]s, '''Satake diagrams''' are a generalization of [[Dynkin diagram|Dynkin diagrams]] that classify involutions of root systems that are relevant in several contexts. They were introduced in {{harvtxt|Satake|1960|p=109}} and were originally used to classify [[real form (Lie theory)|real simple Lie algebras]]. Additionally, they also classify symmetric pairs <math>(\mathfrak{g},\mathfrak{k})</math> of Lie algebras, where <math>\mathfrak{g}</math> is semisimple.

More concretely, given a complex semisimple Lie algebra <math>\mathfrak{g}</math>, the Satake diagrams made from <math>\mathfrak{g}</math>'s Dynkin diagram classify the involutions of <math>\mathfrak{g}</math>'s [[root system]] that extend to an anti-linear involutive automorphism {{mvar|&sigma;}} of <math>\mathfrak{g}</math>.{{sfn|Araki|1962}} The fixed points <math>\mathfrak{g}^\sigma</math> are then a real form of <math>\mathfrak{g}</math>. The same Satake diagrams also classify the involutions of <math>\mathfrak{g}</math>'s root system that extend to a (linear) involutive automorphism {{mvar|&sigma;}} of <math>\mathfrak{g}</math>.{{sfn|Kolb|2014|loc=Theorem 2.7}} The fixed points <math>\mathfrak{k}</math> form a complex Lie subalgebra of <math>\mathfrak{g}</math>, so that <math>(\mathfrak{g},\mathfrak{k})</math> is a symmetric pair.

More generally, the '''Tits index''' or '''Satake–Tits diagram''' of a reductive [[algebraic group]] over a field is a generalization of the Satake diagram to arbitrary fields, introduced by {{harvtxt|Tits|1966}}, that reduces the classification of reductive algebraic groups to that of [[Linear algebraic group#Examples|anisotropic]] [[Reductive group|reductive]] algebraic groups.

Satake diagrams are distinct from [[Vogan diagram]]s although they look similar.

== Definition ==
Let {{mvar|V}} be a real vector space. A '''&sigma;-root system'''{{sfn|Araki|1962|loc=§2}} <math>(R,\sigma)</math> consists of a root system <math>R\subset V</math> that spans {{mvar|V}} and a linear involution {{mvar|&sigma;}} of {{mvar|V}} that satisfies <math>\sigma(R)=R</math>.

Let <math>R_\bullet\subset R</math> be the set of roots fixed by {{mvar|&sigma;}} and let
<math display="block">\Sigma := \left\{ \frac{\alpha-\sigma(\alpha)}{2}: \alpha\in R\setminus R_\bullet\right\}.</math> {{mvar|&Sigma;}} is called the '''[[restricted root system]]'''. 

The '''Satake diagram''' of a &sigma;-root system <math>(R,\sigma)</math> is obtained as follows: Let <math>\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n</math> be simple roots of {{mvar|R}} such that <math>\alpha_{n+1-p},\dots,\alpha_n</math> are simple roots of <math>R_\bullet</math>. We can define an involution {{mvar|&tau;}} of <math>\{1,\dots,n-p\}</math> by having
<math display="block">\sigma(\alpha_i) = \alpha_{\tau(i)} + \Z R_\bullet\qquad
(i=1,\dots,n-p).</math> The Satake diagram is then obtained from the Dynkin diagram describing {{mvar|R}} by blackening the vertices corresponding to <math>\alpha_{n+1-p},\dots,\alpha_n</math>, and by drawing arrows between the white vertices that are interchanged by {{mvar|&tau;}}.

=== Satake diagram of a real semisimple Lie algebra ===
Let <math>\mathfrak{g}_\R</math> be a real semisimple Lie algebra and let <math>\mathfrak{g}=\mathfrak{g}_\R\otimes\C</math> be its complexification. Define the map
<math display="block">\sigma:\mathfrak{g}\to\mathfrak{g},\qquad
X\otimes z\mapsto X\otimes\overline{z}.</math>
This is an anti-linear involutive automorphism of real Lie algebras and its fixed-point set is our original <math>\mathfrak{g}_\R</math>.

Let <math>\mathfrak{h}\le\mathfrak{g}</math> be a [[Cartan subalgebra]] that satisfies <math>\sigma(\mathfrak{h})=\mathfrak{h}</math> and is maximally split, i.e. when we split <math>\mathfrak{h}</math> into {{mvar|&sigma;}}-eigenspaces, the <math>-1</math>-eigenspace has maximal dimension. {{mvar|&sigma;}} induces an anti-linear involution {{mvar|&sigma;*}} on <math>\mathfrak{h}^*</math>:
<math display="block">\sigma^*(\lambda)(v) = \overline{\lambda(\sigma(v))}\qquad
(\lambda\in\mathfrak{h}^*,v\in\mathfrak{h}).</math> 
If <math>X\in\mathfrak{g}_\alpha</math> is a root vector, one can show that
<math>\sigma(X)\in\mathfrak{g}_{\sigma^*(\alpha)}</math>. Consequently, {{mvar|&sigma;*}} preserves
the root system {{mvar|R}} of <math>\mathfrak{g}</math>. We thus obtain a &sigma;-root system <math>(R,\sigma^*)</math> whose Satake diagram is the Satake diagram of <math>\mathfrak{g}_\R</math>.

=== Satake diagram of a symmetric pair ===
Let <math>(\mathfrak{g},\mathfrak{k})</math> be a symmetric pair of complex Lie algebras where <math>\mathfrak{g}</math> is semisimple, i.e. let
{{mvar|&theta;}} be an involutive Lie algebra automorphism of <math>\mathfrak{g}</math> and let
<math>\mathfrak{k}</math> be its fixed-point set. It is shown in {{harvtxt|Kolb|2014|loc=Appendix A}} that these symmetric pairs (even for <math>\mathfrak{g}</math> an infinite-dimensional [[Kac-Moody algebra]]), or equivalently these involutive automorphisms, can be classified using
so-called admissible pairs. These admissible pairs describe again a &sigma;-root system that can be obtained from the automorphism {{mvar|&sigma;}}, and the Satake diagrams that arise this way are exactly{{sfn|Kolb|2014|loc=below Definition 2.3}} the ones listed in {{harvtxt|Araki|1962|pp=32,33}} and the Satake diagrams obtained by blackening all vertices.

'''Definition'''{{sfn|Kolb|2014|loc=§2.4}}
Given a Dynkin diagram with vertex set {{mvar|I}}, an '''admissible pair''' <math>(I_\bullet, \tau)</math> consists of a subset <math>I_\bullet</math> of finite type and a diagram automorphism {{mvar|&tau;}} satisfying
* <math>\tau^2=\operatorname{id}</math>
* <math>\tau(I_\bullet)=I_\bullet</math>
* The permutation <math>\tau|_{I_\bullet}</math> coincides with <math>-w_\bullet</math> (where <math>w_\bullet</math> is the longest element of the Weyl group generated by the vertices in <math>I_\bullet</math>)
* For <math>j\in I\setminus I_\bullet</math> with <math>\tau(i)=i</math>, we have <math>\alpha_j(\rho^\vee_\bullet)\in\Z</math>, where <math display="block">\rho^\vee_\bullet = \frac{1}{2}\sum_{\alpha\in R_\bullet^+} \alpha^\vee.</math>

Given an admissible pair <math>(I_\bullet,\tau)</math>, we can define a &sigma;-root system by equipping the root system {{mvar|R}} of {{mvar|I}} with the involution <math>\sigma = -w_\bullet\circ\tau</math>

== Classification of Satake diagrams ==
In {{harvtxt|Araki|1962|loc=§5}} it is proven that every Satake diagram arising from a real semisimple Lie algebra (equivalently: symmetric pair <math>(\mathfrak{g},\mathfrak{k})</math> with <math>\mathfrak{g}</math> semisimple) is a disconnected union of
* two times the same Dynkin diagram (with white vertices), with arrows matching the vertices
* one of the following diagrams:

== Examples ==
{{Expand section|date=December 2009}}
* [[Compact Lie algebra]]s correspond to the Satake diagram with all vertices blackened. This corresponds to the symmetric pair <math>(\mathfrak{g},\mathfrak{g})</math>
* [[Split Lie algebra]]s correspond to the Satake diagram with only white (i.e., non blackened) and unpaired vertices.
* A table can be found at {{Harv|Onishchik|Vinberg|1994|loc=[https://books.google.com/books?id=l8nJCNiIQAAC&pg=PA229 Table 4, pp. 229–230]}}.

== Differences between Satake and Vogan diagrams ==
Both Satake and [[Vogan diagram]]s are used to classify semisimple Lie groups or algebras (or algebraic groups) over the reals and both consist of Dynkin diagrams enriched by blackening a subset of the nodes and connecting some pairs of vertices by arrows.  Satake diagrams, however, can be generalized to any field (see above) and fall under the general paradigm of [[Galois cohomology]], whereas Vogan diagrams are defined specifically over the reals.  Generally speaking, the structure of a real semisimple Lie algebra is encoded in a more transparent way in its Satake diagram, but Vogan diagrams are simpler to classify.

The essential difference is that the Satake diagram of a real semisimple Lie algebra <math>\mathfrak{g}</math> with [[Cartan decomposition|Cartan involution]] ''θ'' and associated Cartan pair <math>\mathfrak{g} = \mathfrak{k} \oplus \mathfrak{p}</math> (the +1 and −1 eigenspaces of ''θ'') is defined by starting from a maximally noncompact ''θ''-stable [[Cartan subalgebra]] <math>\mathfrak{h}</math>, that is, one for which <math>\theta(\mathfrak{h})=\mathfrak{h}</math> and <math>\mathfrak{h}\cap\mathfrak{k}</math> is as small as possible (in the presentation above, <math>\mathfrak{h}</math> appears as the Lie algebra of the maximal split torus ''S''), whereas Vogan diagrams are defined starting from a maximally compact ''θ''-stable Cartan subalgebra, that is, one for which <math>\theta(\mathfrak{h})=\mathfrak{h}</math> and <math>\mathfrak{h}\cap\mathfrak{k}</math> is as large as possible.

The unadorned Dynkin diagram (i.e., that with only white nodes and no arrows), when interpreted as a Satake diagram, represents the split real form of the Lie algebra, whereas it represents the compact form when interpreted as a Vogan diagram.

== Generalisation: Satake—Tits diagrams ==

Suppose that ''G'' is an algebraic group defined over a field ''k'', such as the reals. We let ''S'' be a maximal split torus in ''G'', and take ''T'' to be a maximal torus containing ''S'' defined over the separable algebraic closure ''K'' of ''k''. Then ''G''(''K'') has a Dynkin diagram with respect to some choice of positive roots of ''T''. This Dynkin diagram has a natural action of the Galois group of ''K''/''k''. Also some of the simple roots vanish on ''S''. The '''Satake–Tits diagram''' is given by the Dynkin diagram ''D'', together with the action of the Galois group, with the simple roots vanishing on ''S'' colored black. In the case when ''k'' is the field of real numbers, the absolute Galois group has order 2, and its action on ''D'' is represented by drawing conjugate points of the Dynkin diagram near each other, and the Satake–Tits diagram is called a Satake diagram.
